questiontext.text: A test level is a group of test activities that are organised primarily by:

answer.text: When they happen and what scope they cover in the development lifecycle (unit, integration, system, acceptance)

feedback.text: Correct — a level is defined by scope/when: unit, integration, system, acceptance.

answer.text: The quality attribute or objective they target (functional, performance, security)

feedback.text: That describes a test type, not a level.

answer.text: The programming language used to write the tests

feedback.text: Levels are not defined by tooling or language.

answer.text: Whether the tester is internal or external to the company

feedback.text: Who runs the test does not define a level; scope and lifecycle position do.

generalfeedback.text: Test levels are groups of activities organised by scope and position in the lifecycle: unit/component, integration, system, and acceptance. They answer "when/at what scope", distinct from test types, which answer "what quality attribute".

questiontext.text: A test type is a group of test activities organised primarily by:

answer.text: The specific quality characteristic or objective being evaluated (e.g. functional, performance, security)

feedback.text: Correct — a type is defined by the objective/attribute under test.

answer.text: Its position in the lifecycle (unit, integration, system, acceptance)

feedback.text: That describes a test level, not a type.

answer.text: The number of testers assigned to it

feedback.text: Team size does not define a test type.

answer.text: The order in which defects are reported

feedback.text: Defect reporting order is unrelated to how types are defined.

generalfeedback.text: Test types group activities by the objective or quality attribute they evaluate — functional, non-functional, structural (white-box), and change-related. They answer "what are we testing for", distinct from levels, which answer "at what scope/when".

name.text: The four test levels in order

questiontext.text: Which sequence lists the classic test levels in their usual order?

answer.text: Unit/component → integration → system → acceptance

feedback.text: Correct — this is the standard ordering of test levels.

answer.text: Functional → non-functional → structural → change-related

feedback.text: Those are test types, not levels.

answer.text: Acceptance → system → integration → unit

feedback.text: This reverses the order; unit testing comes first.

answer.text: Smoke → regression → performance → security

feedback.text: These are test types/activities, not the four levels.

generalfeedback.text: The four classic test levels run from smallest to largest scope: unit/component, then integration, then system, then acceptance.

questiontext.text: Functional testing evaluates:

answer.text: What the system does — the functions and behaviour it is supposed to provide

feedback.text: Correct — functional testing checks "what" the system does.

answer.text: How well the system performs a function — its speed, security, or usability

feedback.text: That is non-functional testing (the "how well" qualities).

answer.text: The internal code structure and coverage achieved

feedback.text: That is structural (white-box) testing.

answer.text: Whether a fix re-broke previously working features

feedback.text: That is change-related (regression) testing.

generalfeedback.text: Functional testing asks "does it do what it is supposed to do?" — it evaluates the functions/behaviour. Non-functional testing asks "how well?" — performance, security, usability, and other quality attributes.

questiontext.text: Which of the following is a non-functional test type?

answer.text: Performance (load/stress) testing

feedback.text: Correct — performance is a non-functional quality attribute.

answer.text: Checking that "add to cart" adds the chosen item

feedback.text: That is functional testing — it checks what the system does.

answer.text: Measuring statement coverage of the code

feedback.text: That is structural (white-box) testing, not non-functional.

answer.text: Re-running a failed test after the defect is fixed

feedback.text: That is confirmation testing, a change-related activity.

generalfeedback.text: Non-functional types evaluate "how well" — performance, security, usability, reliability, compatibility, portability, maintainability. Performance (including load and stress) is a classic example.

questiontext.text: Confirmation (re-)testing means:

answer.text: Re-running the test that originally revealed a defect, after the fix, to confirm the defect is gone

feedback.text: Correct — confirmation testing verifies that the specific fix worked.

answer.text: Running other tests to check the fix did not break anything else

feedback.text: That is regression testing, not confirmation testing.

answer.text: A first quick check that the build is stable enough to test

feedback.text: That is smoke testing.

answer.text: Testing the system against user business needs before go-live

feedback.text: That is acceptance testing, a level, not confirmation testing.

generalfeedback.text: Confirmation testing (re-testing) re-executes the exact test case that failed, now that the defect is supposedly fixed, to confirm the fix. Checking for unintended side effects elsewhere is the separate activity of regression testing.

questiontext.text: Regression testing means:

answer.text: Re-testing previously working functionality to detect unintended side effects introduced by a change

feedback.text: Correct — regression guards against a change breaking things that used to work.

answer.text: Re-running only the one test that failed, to confirm the specific fix

feedback.text: That is confirmation (re-)testing, not regression.

answer.text: Testing a brand-new feature for the first time

feedback.text: Testing new functionality is not regression testing; regression re-checks existing behaviour.

answer.text: Measuring how fast the system responds under load

feedback.text: That is performance testing, a non-functional type.

generalfeedback.text: Regression testing re-executes tests over already-working functionality after a change (a fix, enhancement, or configuration change) to catch unintended side effects. It is a change-related test type performed across levels.

questiontext.text: Smoke testing is best described as:

answer.text: A quick, shallow set of checks confirming the build's main functions work well enough to justify further testing

feedback.text: Correct — smoke testing is a broad, shallow "is the build stable?" check.

answer.text: An exhaustive re-run of the entire test suite after every change

feedback.text: That would be full regression testing, not a quick smoke test.

answer.text: A deep test of one specific area after a small change

feedback.text: That describes sanity testing, which is narrow and deep rather than broad and shallow.

answer.text: Validation of the system against user requirements before release

feedback.text: That is acceptance testing, a level, not smoke testing.

generalfeedback.text: A smoke test is a small, broad, shallow set of checks (often automated as build verification) run to decide whether a build is stable enough to spend more testing effort on it.

questiontext.text: The distinguishing feature of static testing is that it:

answer.text: Examines the work product without executing the code (reviews, static analysis)

feedback.text: Correct — static testing evaluates artefacts without running them.

answer.text: Runs the software and observes its behaviour on inputs

feedback.text: That is dynamic testing, the opposite of static.

answer.text: Can only be applied at the acceptance level

feedback.text: Static testing (reviews, analysis) can apply throughout, and it is defined by not executing code.

answer.text: Requires measuring code coverage

feedback.text: Coverage is a dynamic/structural concern; static testing does not run the code.

generalfeedback.text: Static testing evaluates work products (code, requirements, designs) without executing them — via reviews and static analysis. Dynamic testing executes the software and observes actual behaviour.

name.text: Classify: testing one function in isolation

questiontext.text: A developer tests a single function in isolation, checking its logic directly. Which test level is this?

answer.text: Unit (component) testing

feedback.text: Correct — testing an individual component in isolation is the unit level.

answer.text: Integration testing

feedback.text: Integration testing checks interactions between components, not one component alone.

answer.text: System testing

feedback.text: System testing exercises the whole integrated system, not a single function.

answer.text: Acceptance testing

feedback.text: Acceptance testing validates the finished system against user needs, not an isolated function.

generalfeedback.text: Exercising an individual component/function in isolation is unit (component) testing — the smallest-scope level.

questiontext.text: A team measures how quickly the application responds when many users hit it at once. Which test type is this?

answer.text: Performance testing (a non-functional type)

feedback.text: Correct — measuring response under load is non-functional performance testing.

answer.text: Functional testing

feedback.text: Functional testing checks what the system does, not how fast it does it.

answer.text: Acceptance (a level, wrongly named here)

feedback.text: Acceptance is a level, not the type being described; and this activity is performance testing.

answer.text: Confirmation testing

feedback.text: Confirmation testing re-checks a fix; it does not measure response time.

generalfeedback.text: Measuring speed/throughput under load evaluates a quality attribute (performance), so it is a non-functional test type — and it can be applied at any level (commonly system).

questiontext.text: Before release, the intended users try the system against their real business needs to decide whether to accept it. Which test level is this?

answer.text: Acceptance testing

feedback.text: Correct — user validation against business needs prior to acceptance is the acceptance level.

answer.text: Unit testing

feedback.text: Unit testing checks a single component, not the whole system against user needs.

answer.text: Integration testing

feedback.text: Integration testing checks module interactions, not user acceptance.

answer.text: Performance testing

feedback.text: Performance is a non-functional type, not a level; this activity is acceptance-level validation.

generalfeedback.text: Validating the completed system against user requirements and business processes to establish confidence for release is acceptance testing — the last of the four levels.

questiontext.text: Structural (white-box) testing is characterised by:

answer.text: Deriving and measuring tests from the internal structure of the code (e.g. statement or branch coverage)

feedback.text: Correct — structural testing works from the code's internal structure and coverage.

answer.text: Deriving tests only from the specification, ignoring the code

feedback.text: That is black-box (specification-based) testing, not structural.

answer.text: Measuring the system's response time under load

feedback.text: That is performance testing, a non-functional type.

answer.text: Re-running earlier tests after a change

feedback.text: That is regression testing, a change-related type.

generalfeedback.text: Structural (white-box) testing uses the internal structure of the item — control flow, data flow — to derive tests and to measure coverage (statement, branch, etc.). It is a distinct test type that can be applied at any level.

name.text: Functional testing checks what the system does

questiontext.text: Functional testing evaluates what the system does (its functions), while non-functional testing evaluates how well it does it.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — functional = what it does; non-functional = how well it does it.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: This is the standard distinction: functional targets behaviour/functions, non-functional targets quality attributes.

generalfeedback.text: Functional testing checks the functions and behaviour the system provides; non-functional testing checks quality attributes such as performance, security, usability and reliability — "how well" those functions are delivered.

name.text: Which item is a test level, not a type

questiontext.text: Which of the following is a test level (not a test type)?

answer.text: Acceptance

feedback.text: Correct — acceptance is a test level (scope/when).

answer.text: Performance

feedback.text: Performance is a non-functional test type, not a level.

answer.text: Security

feedback.text: Security is a non-functional test type, not a level.

answer.text: Regression

feedback.text: Regression is a change-related test type, not a level.

generalfeedback.text: Acceptance is one of the four levels (unit, integration, system, acceptance). Performance, security, and regression are all test types (non-functional or change-related), not levels.

name.text: Test basis for the unit level

questiontext.text: Which document is the usual test basis for unit (component) testing?

answer.text: The detailed (low-level) design and the code of the component

feedback.text: Correct — unit testing is based on the component's detailed design and code.

answer.text: The system requirements specification

feedback.text: That is the basis for system testing, not unit testing.

answer.text: The user requirements and business processes

feedback.text: That is the basis for acceptance testing.

answer.text: The software architecture and interface specifications

feedback.text: That is the basis for integration testing.

generalfeedback.text: Each level draws on a different test basis. Unit testing is based on the detailed/component design and the code itself, since it targets the internals of a single component.

name.text: Test basis for the system level

questiontext.text: Which document is the usual test basis for system testing?

answer.text: The system/software requirements specification (functional and non-functional)

feedback.text: Correct — system testing is based on the system requirements.

answer.text: The component's detailed design and code

feedback.text: That is the basis for unit testing.

answer.text: The software architecture and module interfaces

feedback.text: That is the basis for integration testing.

answer.text: The legal contract signed with the customer

feedback.text: That belongs to (contractual) acceptance testing, not system testing.

generalfeedback.text: System testing verifies the complete, integrated system against its specified requirements, so the system/software requirements specification (both functional and non-functional) is its test basis.

name.text: Is acceptance a level or a type?

questiontext.text: On the level-vs-type axes, acceptance testing is:

answer.text: A test level (defined by scope/when in the lifecycle)

feedback.text: Correct — acceptance is the fourth test level.

answer.text: A non-functional test type

feedback.text: Acceptance is a level; functional and non-functional types can both be run within it.

answer.text: A structural test type

feedback.text: Acceptance is not a type at all; it is a level.

answer.text: A change-related test type

feedback.text: Change-related types are confirmation and regression; acceptance is a level.

generalfeedback.text: Acceptance sits on the level axis (unit, integration, system, acceptance). Within it you may still run functional and non-functional test types — the two axes are orthogonal.

name.text: Is performance a level or a type?

questiontext.text: On the level-vs-type axes, performance testing is:

answer.text: A non-functional test type (it can be run at several levels)

feedback.text: Correct — performance is a non-functional type, not a level.

answer.text: A test level between system and acceptance

feedback.text: There is no "performance level"; the levels are unit, integration, system, acceptance.

answer.text: A test level that replaces system testing

feedback.text: Performance is a type; it does not sit on the level axis at all.

answer.text: A change-related test type

feedback.text: Change-related types are confirmation and regression; performance is non-functional.

generalfeedback.text: Performance is a non-functional test type. A common misconception treats it as a level, but it is an objective (a quality attribute) that can be pursued at unit, integration, system, or acceptance level.

name.text: Is integration a level or a type?

questiontext.text: On the level-vs-type axes, integration testing is:

answer.text: A test level (its scope is the interactions between components or systems)

feedback.text: Correct — integration is the second test level.

answer.text: A non-functional test type

feedback.text: Integration is a level; non-functional types can be run within it.

answer.text: A change-related test type

feedback.text: Change-related types are confirmation and regression; integration is a level.

answer.text: A structural test type

feedback.text: Integration is defined by scope (interfaces), which makes it a level, not a type.

generalfeedback.text: Integration is a test level: its scope is the interfaces and interactions between components (component integration) or between systems (system integration).

name.text: Is security a level or a type?

questiontext.text: On the level-vs-type axes, security testing is:

answer.text: A non-functional test type

feedback.text: Correct — security is a non-functional quality attribute, hence a type.

answer.text: A test level after acceptance

feedback.text: There is no security level; the levels end at acceptance.

answer.text: A structural test type

feedback.text: Security is non-functional, not structural (structural = coverage of code).

answer.text: A change-related test type

feedback.text: Change-related types are confirmation and regression; security is non-functional.

generalfeedback.text: Security is a non-functional test type (protecting against threats, controlling access). Like other types, it can be applied at multiple levels — for instance security testing at the system level.

questiontext.text: A defect was fixed. Which activity re-runs the exact test that had failed to check the fix itself?

answer.text: Confirmation (re-)testing

feedback.text: Correct — confirmation testing re-executes the failed test to verify the fix.

answer.text: Regression testing

feedback.text: Regression checks that nothing else broke; it is not the re-run of the specific failed test.

answer.text: Smoke testing

feedback.text: Smoke testing is a broad build-stability check, not verification of a specific fix.

answer.text: System testing

feedback.text: System testing is a level; the activity described is confirmation testing.

generalfeedback.text: Confirmation testing re-executes the previously failing test after the fix to confirm the defect is resolved. Regression testing is the complementary activity of checking for unintended side effects elsewhere.

questiontext.text: After a fix, which activity re-runs other, previously passing tests to check nothing else broke?

answer.text: Regression testing

feedback.text: Correct — regression testing detects unintended side effects of the change.

answer.text: Confirmation (re-)testing

feedback.text: Confirmation re-runs the one failed test to verify the fix, not the surrounding tests.

answer.text: Sanity testing

feedback.text: Sanity testing is a narrow, quick check of one area, not broad side-effect detection.

answer.text: Acceptance testing

feedback.text: Acceptance is a level about user validation, not side-effect detection after a fix.

generalfeedback.text: Regression testing re-runs previously passing tests to catch unintended side effects introduced by a change. Confirmation testing is the narrower re-run of the specific test that had failed.

name.text: A type applied at a level

questiontext.text: "Performance testing carried out at the system level" is best understood as:

answer.text: A non-functional test type (performance) applied at a particular test level (system)

feedback.text: Correct — level and type are orthogonal, so a type is applied at a level.

answer.text: A contradiction, because performance and system are two names for the same thing

feedback.text: They are on different axes (type vs level), so there is no contradiction.

answer.text: Two separate test levels performed together

feedback.text: Performance is a type, not a level, so this is not two levels.

answer.text: A change-related activity

feedback.text: Performance is non-functional, not change-related.

generalfeedback.text: Because levels (when/scope) and types (which quality attribute) are orthogonal axes, any type can be run at any level. "Performance testing at system level" names the type (performance) and the level (system) together.

name.text: Which level checks interfaces between components?

questiontext.text: Which level's scope is specifically the interfaces and interactions between components that have already been unit-tested?

answer.text: Integration testing

feedback.text: Correct — component integration testing targets interfaces between components.

answer.text: Unit testing

feedback.text: Unit testing checks one component in isolation, not the interfaces between them.

answer.text: System testing

feedback.text: System testing checks the whole integrated system's behaviour, not just component interfaces.

answer.text: Acceptance testing

feedback.text: Acceptance validates the finished system against user needs, not component interfaces.

generalfeedback.text: Integration testing (component integration) sits between unit and system testing; its scope is the interactions and interfaces between components that have already passed unit testing.

name.text: Test basis for the acceptance level

questiontext.text: Which is the usual test basis for acceptance testing?

answer.text: User requirements, business processes, and (where relevant) contracts or regulations

feedback.text: Correct — acceptance testing is based on user/business needs and any contractual/regulatory requirements.

answer.text: The component's code and detailed design

feedback.text: That is the basis for unit testing.

answer.text: The software architecture and module interfaces

feedback.text: That is the basis for integration testing.

answer.text: Statement- and branch-coverage reports

feedback.text: Coverage reports are a structural-testing artefact, not the acceptance test basis.

generalfeedback.text: Acceptance testing establishes confidence for release, so its test basis is user requirements, business processes and rules, use cases, and any contractual or regulatory requirements.

name.text: Test basis for the integration level

questiontext.text: Which is the usual test basis for integration testing?

answer.text: The software and system design, architecture, and interface specifications

feedback.text: Correct — integration testing is based on the design/architecture and interfaces.

answer.text: The user requirements and business processes

feedback.text: That is the basis for acceptance testing.

answer.text: The component's code alone

feedback.text: Code alone is closer to the unit-testing basis; integration draws on design and interfaces.

answer.text: The signed customer contract

feedback.text: That belongs to contractual acceptance testing, not integration.

generalfeedback.text: Integration testing targets how components/systems fit together, so its test basis is the software and system design, the architecture, workflows, and interface specifications.

name.text: At which levels can regression be done?

questiontext.text: At which test level(s) can regression testing be performed?

answer.text: At any level — unit, integration, system, or acceptance

feedback.text: Correct — regression is a change-related type applied across all levels.

answer.text: Only at the acceptance level

feedback.text: Regression is not tied to acceptance; it is run wherever a change could cause side effects.

answer.text: Only at the system level

feedback.text: Regression applies at every level, not just system.

answer.text: It is itself a level, so the question does not apply

feedback.text: Regression is a change-related test type, not a level.

generalfeedback.text: Regression testing is a change-related test type. Because types are orthogonal to levels, regression can and should be performed at any level where a change might have introduced side effects.

questiontext.text: Performance testing is one of the standard test levels.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Incorrect — performance is a non-functional test type, not a level. The levels are unit, integration, system, and acceptance.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: Correct — performance is a non-functional test type, not a level.

generalfeedback.text: The four levels are unit, integration, system, and acceptance. Performance is a non-functional test type that can be applied at any of those levels; it is not itself a level.

questiontext.text: The main purpose of running a smoke test on a new build is to:

answer.text: Quickly decide whether the build is stable enough to warrant further, deeper testing

feedback.text: Correct — smoke testing is a fast go/no-go check on build stability.

answer.text: Exhaustively verify every requirement in detail

feedback.text: That is thorough functional/system testing, not a quick smoke test.

answer.text: Confirm that a specific reported defect has been fixed

feedback.text: That is confirmation testing, not smoke testing.

answer.text: Measure the system's throughput under peak load

feedback.text: That is performance testing, a non-functional type.

generalfeedback.text: A smoke test is a broad, shallow set of checks (often automated) that quickly establishes whether the critical functions of a build work — a gate deciding whether deeper testing is worthwhile.

questiontext.text: Testing backup/restore, installation, and disaster-recovery procedures, performed by operations/administration staff before go-live, is best classified as:

answer.text: Operational acceptance testing (an acceptance-level activity focused on operational readiness)

feedback.text: Correct — operational acceptance (OAT) checks operational readiness at the acceptance level.

answer.text: System testing, because it exercises the whole system

feedback.text: Although it uses the whole system, this is acceptance-level (operational acceptance) work done by operations staff against operational needs, not system-level verification against requirements.

answer.text: Unit testing of the backup component

feedback.text: OAT exercises operational procedures on the whole system, not an isolated component.

answer.text: Regression testing

feedback.text: OAT is about operational readiness, not re-checking for side effects of a change.

generalfeedback.text: Operational acceptance testing (OAT) is a form of acceptance testing carried out by operations/system-administration staff to confirm the system is ready to operate — backup/restore, install/uninstall, maintenance, disaster recovery, and security procedures. It is distinct from system testing, which verifies the built system against its specified requirements.

questiontext.text: Testing the interfaces between your application and a separate external payment system operated by another organisation is:

answer.text: System integration testing (interactions between distinct systems)

feedback.text: Correct — testing interfaces between separate systems is system integration testing.

answer.text: Component integration testing (interactions between components inside one system)

feedback.text: Component integration is within a single system; here two separate systems interact.

answer.text: Unit testing of the payment module

feedback.text: This concerns cross-system interfaces, not a single component in isolation.

answer.text: Acceptance testing

feedback.text: This targets the interface between systems, an integration concern, not user acceptance.

generalfeedback.text: Integration testing has two sub-forms. Component integration testing checks interactions between components within one system (after unit testing). System integration testing checks interactions between different systems or with external services (often after system testing).

questiontext.text: Which statement correctly separates usability testing from user acceptance testing (UAT)?

answer.text: Usability is a non-functional test type (how easy the system is to use); UAT is a test level (users deciding whether to accept the system)

feedback.text: Correct — one is a type (quality attribute), the other is a level (lifecycle stage).

answer.text: Both are test levels performed one after the other

feedback.text: Usability is a type, not a level; only UAT is a level.

answer.text: Both are non-functional test types

feedback.text: Usability is a non-functional type, but UAT is a level, not a type.

answer.text: Usability is a level and UAT is a type

feedback.text: This reverses them: usability is the type and UAT is the level.

generalfeedback.text: Usability testing evaluates a quality attribute (ease of use), so it is a non-functional test type and can run at various levels. User acceptance testing is a test level — the stage where users validate the system against their needs — and it may itself include usability checks.

name.text: Why type is orthogonal to level

questiontext.text: What does it mean to say test types are orthogonal to test levels?

answer.text: Any test type can, in principle, be performed at any test level — the two classifications are independent

feedback.text: Correct — orthogonal means the axes vary independently, so any type pairs with any level.

answer.text: Each test level is permanently tied to exactly one test type

feedback.text: That is the opposite of orthogonal; orthogonality means they are independent.

answer.text: Test types replace test levels once the system is integrated

feedback.text: Types do not replace levels; the two coexist as independent axes.

answer.text: Only functional testing can be done at more than one level

feedback.text: All types — functional, non-functional, structural, change-related — can span levels.

generalfeedback.text: "Orthogonal" means the level axis (when/scope) and the type axis (which quality attribute/objective) vary independently. So functional, non-functional, structural, and change-related types can each be applied at unit, integration, system, or acceptance level.

questiontext.text: Which description correctly distinguishes smoke, sanity, and regression testing?

answer.text: Smoke = broad shallow build-stability check; sanity = narrow deep check of one area after a small change; regression = re-testing existing functionality for side effects of a change

feedback.text: Correct — smoke is broad/shallow, sanity is narrow/deep, regression re-checks prior functionality.

answer.text: All three mean the same thing: re-running the full test suite

feedback.text: They differ in breadth, depth, and purpose; they are not synonyms.

answer.text: Smoke tests one area deeply; sanity checks the whole build shallowly; regression tests new features

feedback.text: This swaps smoke and sanity, and regression targets existing functionality, not new features.

answer.text: Smoke and sanity are levels; regression is a type

feedback.text: All three are test activities/types, not levels.

generalfeedback.text: Smoke testing is a broad, shallow check that a build's key functions work (build stability). Sanity testing is a narrow, deep check of a specific area after a small change. Regression testing re-tests previously working functionality across a change to detect unintended side effects.

name.text: Match level to its test basis

questiontext.text: Which pairing of level to test basis is correct?

answer.text: System testing → system/software requirements specification

feedback.text: Correct — system testing is based on the system requirements.

answer.text: Unit testing → user requirements and business processes

feedback.text: User requirements/business processes are the acceptance basis; unit testing uses code and detailed design.

answer.text: Acceptance testing → component code and detailed design

feedback.text: Component code/detailed design is the unit-testing basis; acceptance uses user/business requirements.

answer.text: Integration testing → statement-coverage reports

feedback.text: Coverage reports are structural artefacts; integration's basis is design, architecture, and interfaces.

generalfeedback.text: Test basis by level: unit → code/detailed design; integration → design/architecture/interfaces; system → system/software requirements; acceptance → user requirements/business processes (and contracts/regulations). Only the system pairing is correct here.

questiontext.text: Regression testing is one of the four test levels.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Incorrect — regression is a change-related test type performed across levels, not a level itself.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: Correct — regression is a change-related test type, not one of the levels.

generalfeedback.text: The four levels are unit, integration, system, and acceptance. Regression (like confirmation) is a change-related test type that can be run at any of those levels; it is not itself a level.

questiontext.text: Which statement about the types exercised during system testing is correct?

answer.text: System testing can include both functional and non-functional types (e.g. behaviour against requirements plus performance and security)

feedback.text: Correct — a level can host multiple types; system testing typically covers functional and non-functional.

answer.text: System testing is purely functional and never non-functional

feedback.text: System testing routinely includes non-functional types such as performance and security.

answer.text: System testing is purely non-functional and never functional

feedback.text: System testing also verifies functional behaviour against requirements.

answer.text: System testing is itself a test type, so the question of types does not apply

feedback.text: System testing is a level; multiple types are exercised within it.

generalfeedback.text: Because levels and types are orthogonal, a single level hosts several types. System testing commonly combines functional testing (behaviour against requirements) with non-functional testing (performance, security, reliability, etc.).

name.text: Classify: patch verified, then suite re-run

questiontext.text: After a bug fix, the tester first re-runs the exact failing test, then re-runs the surrounding suite of previously passing tests. These two activities are, respectively:

answer.text: Confirmation testing, then regression testing

feedback.text: Correct — re-running the failed test is confirmation; re-running the rest is regression.

answer.text: Regression testing, then confirmation testing

feedback.text: This reverses them: the specific failed test is confirmation, the surrounding suite is regression.

answer.text: Smoke testing, then sanity testing

feedback.text: Neither activity is a build-stability or narrow-area check; they are the change-related pair.

answer.text: Two runs of the same acceptance test

feedback.text: These are change-related type activities, not acceptance-level runs.

generalfeedback.text: Confirmation (re-)testing re-runs the specific test that had failed to verify the fix; regression testing then re-runs previously passing tests to ensure the fix caused no unintended side effects. Both are change-related test types.

questiontext.text: Alpha and beta testing are both forms of acceptance testing. What distinguishes them?

answer.text: Alpha is done at the developer's site (by potential users or an independent team); beta is done at the customers' own sites

feedback.text: Correct — alpha at the developer's site, beta in the field at customer sites.

answer.text: Alpha is a test level and beta is a test type

feedback.text: Both are forms of acceptance-level testing, not a level/type split.

answer.text: Alpha tests performance while beta tests functionality

feedback.text: The distinction is location/who, not functional vs non-functional.

answer.text: Alpha is done after release and beta before development

feedback.text: Both occur before general release; the difference is where they are conducted.

generalfeedback.text: Alpha and beta testing are operational/user forms of acceptance testing. Alpha is conducted at the developing organisation's site (by potential users or an independent test team); beta ("field") testing is conducted by real users at their own sites.

questiontext.text: Testing a system against the acceptance criteria written into a signed contract, or against rules imposed by a government regulator, is:

answer.text: Contractual/regulatory acceptance testing (a form of acceptance testing)

feedback.text: Correct — checking against contract or regulation is a form of acceptance testing.

answer.text: Structural testing, because it measures coverage

feedback.text: It validates against contract/regulation, not code coverage.

answer.text: Component integration testing

feedback.text: It concerns acceptance criteria for the whole system, not component interfaces.

answer.text: Confirmation testing

feedback.text: Confirmation re-checks a fix; this is acceptance against contract/regulation.

generalfeedback.text: Contractual acceptance testing verifies the system against acceptance criteria in a contract; regulatory acceptance testing verifies it against laws/regulations (e.g. safety, legal, government standards). Both are forms of the acceptance level.

name.text: Which axis is which in "security testing at acceptance level"

questiontext.text: In the phrase "security testing at the acceptance level", which word names the level and which names the type?

answer.text: "Acceptance" is the level; "security" is the (non-functional) type

feedback.text: Correct — acceptance is the level, security is the non-functional type.

answer.text: "Security" is the level; "acceptance" is the type

feedback.text: This reverses the axes: acceptance is the level, security is the type.

answer.text: Both words name levels

feedback.text: Security is a type, not a level.

answer.text: Both words name types

feedback.text: Acceptance is a level, not a type.

generalfeedback.text: Level = when/scope (acceptance); type = which quality attribute (security, a non-functional type). The phrase pairs one from each orthogonal axis: the security type applied at the acceptance level.

questiontext.text: Which activity is an example of static testing (as opposed to dynamic)?

answer.text: A peer review of the requirements document to find defects before any code runs

feedback.text: Correct — a review inspects a work product without executing code, so it is static testing.

answer.text: Running the program with test inputs and comparing the outputs to expected values

feedback.text: Executing the program is dynamic testing, not static.

answer.text: Measuring branch coverage while the test suite executes

feedback.text: Coverage measured during execution is dynamic (structural) testing.

answer.text: Load-testing the running application with many concurrent users

feedback.text: Load testing executes the system, so it is dynamic (non-functional) testing.

generalfeedback.text: Static testing evaluates a work product without executing code — reviews (of requirements, design, or code) and static analysis. Dynamic testing runs the software; anything that observes running behaviour (including coverage measurement and load testing) is dynamic.

name.text: One type can span multiple levels

questiontext.text: A single test type (for example, functional testing) can be performed at more than one test level.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — because level and type are orthogonal, one type can be applied at several levels (functional testing at unit, integration, system, and acceptance).

answer.text: false

feedback.text: Types and levels are independent axes, so one type can span many levels.

generalfeedback.text: Test types are orthogonal to test levels, so any type may be exercised at any level. Functional testing, for instance, is done at unit, integration, system, and acceptance levels; likewise performance and other non-functional types can span levels.

questiontext.text: Which of the following is a non-functional test type rather than a functional check?

answer.text: Portability testing — verifying the software can be moved to and run in another environment

feedback.text: Correct — portability is a non-functional quality attribute.

answer.text: Verifying that a valid login is accepted and an invalid one rejected

feedback.text: That checks what the system does (behaviour), so it is functional testing.

answer.text: Verifying that a discount is calculated according to the business rules

feedback.text: Calculating the correct result per the rules is a functional check.

answer.text: Verifying that the report contains the required fields

feedback.text: Checking required content/behaviour is functional testing.

generalfeedback.text: Non-functional types evaluate quality attributes — performance, security, usability, reliability, compatibility, portability, maintainability. Portability (moving the software to another environment) is non-functional; the other options check behaviour, which is functional.
